content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the problem of fine-grained source code vulnerability detection and proposes a GNN-based method. Experimental results based on a number of datasets are reported.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
-	Fine-grained vulnerability detection is an important problem.
-	The ideas of modeling the source code via CPG and learning the vulnerability features generally make sense.

Weakness:
-	The novelty of this paper is quite limited. Although fine-grained vulnerability detection is important, this paper fails to state which contributions are original with respect to the state-of-the-art line-level vulnerability detection model (e.g., Ref Li et al., 2021a). In addition, the idea of detecting vulnerability codes via CPG and GNN has already been used in Devign (Ref Zhou et al., 2019). Thus, the novelty of this paper is further reduced.
-	The line-level performance comparison is missing in the experiment. Specifically, the state-of-the-art fine-grained source code vulnerability detection model (e.g., Ref Li et al., 2021a) is missing in the comparison, which brings more concerns about the performance improvement of the proposed method.
-	The rationale behind the design of the Influence Score remains unclear. The Influence Score computed by Formula (4) is designed to alleviate the over-smoothing problem in GCN and filter out those vulnerable lines of code by simply adding a learnable parameter to the node features. More discussion and empirical evidence (e.g., the ablation study) should be provided about how the added bias works.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty of this paper is quite limited. The rationale behind the design of the Influence Score remains unclear. The line-level performance comparison is missing in the experiment. See the Weakness for details.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a GNN-based approach to identify software
vulnerabilities at the source code level. To this end, they rely on a
multidimensional program features built on top of code property graphs
to capture vulnerability patterns and generalize accordingly. The
authors evaluated their approach on 13 real-world projects; not only
their approach outperforms the state-of-the-art, but it also provides
actionable points (e.g., vulnerability location) for helping developers
to fix the underlying security issues.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ Focus on the identification of the location of vulnerabilities
+ Build on CPGs and rely on GNN to capture logic and structural code information
+ Large-scale experiments

- Lack of comparison against the state-of-the-art
- Lack of details in the methodology
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written, and the work is novel although poorly motivated and positioned against the state-of-the-art. There are fewer details to help reproduce the work entirely.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I find the authors' goal of identifying precise locations of the
vulnerability to be an crucial point of their work. Often, ML-based
vulnerability detection systems exhibit impressive performance but can't
be actioned easily on real datasets.

What does "new vulnerability" mean in this context? Does it mean a new
class of vulnerabilities or a known one (e.g., buffer overflow) that
exhibit a complex pattern that was not observed in the training dataset?
I believe it's the latter but perhaps it would be interesting to clarify
this in the paper. Moreover, it would be interesting to provide some
intuition on how the system is able to generalize across unseen specific
patterns that capture the same vulnerability class. One would expect ML
to pick on known patterns (observed at training time) but because of the
GNN and its latent space, this allows one to learn a vulnerability
pattern's latent representation that generalize well (to unseen ones).
In a way, this is what the authors hint at in the introduction; however,
it'd be great to elaborate on the underlying reasons better.

The authors cite VulDeepecker and others as related work; recent work
has shown how such approaches learned spurious (non-causative) syntactic
features [1]. It would be interesting to understand whether the authors'
approach shares the same limitation. The self-attention network and the
identification of the lines of vulnerabilities are promising; yet,
additional trust could be achieved by understanding what features of the
learned representation are respondible for a given prediction. 

The identification of the location of the vulnerability is showcased on
four projects; do the other projects exhibit similar results or were
those an easy pick? I'd find this outcome fairly important as actionable
points usually hinders ML-based vulnerability detectors. In addition,
what's the Precision of the localization layer? I wonder if it helped
using conformal predictor and outputting a prediction set for a given
confidence level (or significance).

Another point of concern is that the authors cite several prior work but
don't really position theirs against that. There's a sentence at the end
of the related works section that seems to suggest prior work lose code
logic and structural information as it does not build on CPGs (or
similar graphs). While intuitive, this should be assessed with
experiments (or pointing to other works, e.g, [1], that supports this
hypothesis at least partially). Following up on this, how does the
authors' approach outperform (Yamaguchi et al., 2014)?

I believe I failed to understand how labels are given. Is there a ground
truth? I understand the approach learns patterns -- and so it does with
vulnerable code -- but how does it map it to a given label space?

The authors compare their approach against commercial code analysis
tools. I would have expected to see comparisons against Veracode and
Infer (deployed at Meta and open-sourced: https://fbinfer.com/), which
more represent the state-of-the-art. (At least the latter, as Veracode
can be expensive.) In addition, the authors should compare against the
original work of Yamaguchi et al. who introduced CPGs for vulnerability
detection.

Additional comments:

I feel the authors should cite and reference work more thoroughly in the
paper. For instance, they introduce code property graphs in the
introcution but they only reference it in the related work section. This
challenges the understanding of the authors' contributions. 

What is the "total numer of function instances"? Is the underlying
program analysis context-sensitive? A function may be vulnerable in a
given context only.

The authors state they add a CDG and a DDG to the CPG built by Joern.
Aren't those graphs already part of the definition of CPG, which
includes the AST of a given function too?

[1] Arp et al. Dos and Don'ts of Machine Learning for Computer Security. USENIX Security 2022

content.summary_of_the_paper: The proposed method uses GNN to classify vulnerable code both at function and line level. An existing intermediate representation of source code, CFG, is used as an input to the GNN. Nodes of CPGs are encoded using a novel embedding module. A ‘location module’ is introduced, which uses a learnable parameter to provide increased ‘influence scores’ to CFG nodes that are more relevant to vulnerabilities. BiLSTM is used as a readout function to model the dependencies between nodes with high influence scores and predict vulnerabilities at the function level.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Leverages existing source code representation for vulnerability detection to design a GNN based model that identifies vulnerabilities at the function and line level. 
- Experimental results use real world datasets to demonstrate superiority of the proposed method.

Weaknesses
- Although presented as a key innovation, the effectiveness of the ‘location module’ is not well-demonstrated by the experiments. First, there is no ablation study to show the impact of a learnable parameter matrix θ_l. Second, there is no comparative study of the line-level results. Comparison with similar works  (e.g. [1], [2]) would provide more insight about the proposed approach. Third, the ‘false positive’ aspect of detections is not reflected by the two new metrics (hit rate and coverage) used to represent the effectiveness of the line-level detections.
- It seems two new code properties, control and data dependency graph, are integrated with the original properties of CPG. However, there is no justification on why this change is adopted.

[1] Z. Li, D. Zou, S. Xu, Z. Chen, Y. Zhu, and H. Jin, ‘‘VulDeeLocator: A deep learning-based fine-grained vulnerability detector,’’ 2020, arXiv:2001.02350. [Online]. Available: http://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02350

[2] LineVD: Statement-level Vulnerability Detection using Graph Neural Networks David Hin, Andrey Kan, Huaming Chen, M. A. Babar IEEE/ACM 19th International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR) 2022
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novelty
Although GNN based detection approaches have been proposed by previous researchers, this work proposes to use CPG as an input and invents an effective embedding strategy to achieve that goal. The novelty of the work could be expanded to impacting the line-level vulnerability detections. However,  there is no comparative study to support relevant contributions.

Clarity

Overall, the proposed approach is described with relevant details. Some clarifying questions about the evaluation method:
- The model predicts vulnerable functions and/or lines. It is not clear how the precision numbers for each CWE in Table 2 are computed. Are all positive (i.e., vulnerable) predictions considered from the model is counted for each CWE?
- How is the training dataset prepared? Are the models also trained with RD dataset?
- What would be the detection performance of the graph traversal approach using the updated CFG in this work?

Some improvement scopes that did not impact the current review decision:
- It seems Table-2,3 numbers are percentages, which could be explicitly mentioned.
- Use citations for lines like this: “According to statistics, samples from real projects account for only a small proportion of HD”.
- Brief discussions on CPG construct and CWE definitions could be added for increased clarity.

Reproducibility
- Although any implementation is not shared, detailed description of the model along with hyperparameters used for experimental results are provided, which enables reproducibility. 
- This paper uses a new dataset (RD) which contains labeled code from real world projects. Making this new dataset publicly available could potentially help reproducibility as well as future code vulnerability research.
content.summary_of_the_review: Effectiveness of the key contributions of this work around detections of vulnerabilities at line-level are not well-demonstrated because no comparison with relevant work on line-level detections are presented.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a fine-grained source code vulnerability detection model based on GNN to locate vulnerabilities at the function level and the line level. It consists of three modules: embedding module to convert a vulnerable function to a code property graph and further embed this graph, localization module to use layer normalization to rank the most possible error line statement, classification module to use a bilstm followed by GCN to identifiy the function is vulnerable or not.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
   
   - This paper is easy to follow.
   - This paper conducts a more detailed experiment to evaluate the algorithm performance on different projects and CWEs.

Weaknesses:
  
   - The technique novelty is limited. This paper proproses to use code property graph for vulnerability detection is very common and there are many related papers using the similar techniques. Furthermore, the network architecture is also common. Using GCN for learning graph-structured data is not novel.
  - The experiments are also insufficient to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. This paper only compares its performance with some baselines, however we cannot know any other things such as the effect of each module, the hidden size, other GNN variants and so on.
 -  The dataset part is also unclear for me. How to collect the real data in RD dataset, how to label these data, what is the split ratio of train/valid/test, is the dataset available now?

- Novelty: The novelty of this paper is not enough in terms of model design and the experimental results.
- Reproducibility: There is no public resource for the re-implementation.
- Clarity The paper is easy to follow.

content.title: Fine-Grained Source Code Vulnerability Detection via Graph Neural Networks
content.abstract: The number of exploitable vulnerabilities in software continues to increase, the speed of bug fixes and software updates have not increased accordingly. It is therefore crucial to analyze the source code and identify vulnerabilities in the early phase of software development. In this paper, a fine-grained source code vulnerability detection model based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is proposed with the aim of locating vulnerabilities at the function level and line level. First of all, detailed information about the source code is extracted through multi-dimensional program feature encoding to facilitate learning about patterns of vulnerability. Second, extensive experiments are conducted on both a public hybrid dataset and our proposed dataset, which is collected entirely from real software projects. It is demonstrated that our proposed model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods and achieves significant improvements even when faced with more complex real-project source code. Finally, a novel location module is designed to identify potential key vulnerable lines of code. And the effectiveness of the model and its contributions to reducing human workload in practical production are evaluated.
